title: Are Tasers safe enough?: As many as 70 people have died after being zapped by stun guns
article: To tase, or not to tase? That is the question.
Has "tase" been elevated to verb status yet?
Tasers, the electronic stun guns used to subdue violent people, have certainly taken on new crime-fighting status among Canada's police forces.
Kingston police have the $2,000 guns, which shoot 50,000 volts of electricity into a suspect's body, paralysing the person's muscles long enough to handcuff him or her and make an arrest.
But are Tasers (the trade name) as safe as they're touted to be?
When the weapons first came here several years ago, local media representatives volunteered to experience a Taser's effects. They didn't suffer, as far as anyone knows, any long-term effects.

Today, there are questions about the effects of being "tased." A number of incidents in which as many as 70 people in Canada and the United States died after being zapped created a public stir. And that resulted in the report by the Canadian Police Research Centre that was released this week.

Not surprisingly, despite expressing some concerns, the report said Tasers were shown to have been safe in a "vast majority" of the incidents, effectively giving police departments the clearance to keep using the weapons until further information is collected.

On Aug. 8 of last year, 43-year-old Samuel Truscott of Kingston died after being shot with a Taser by city police. Two days later, Ontario's chief coroner determined that the electric shock played no part in
Truscott's death. "His death," said Dr. Jim Cairns, "was due solely due to a drug overdose."

The Truscott case might be considered a textbook case for police use of a Taser. High on cocaine, he was barricaded inside his home, threatening to do harm to himself. When pepper spray failed to stop Truscott, police used the Taser.

Truscott walked, under arrest, to a police cruiser. He was taken to Kingston General Hospital and treated for a cocaine overdose. Two hours later, he went back to hospital and died from effects of the drug.
When the coroner's decision was made public, Kingston Police Chief Bill Closs defended the use of the stun guns as a preferable alternative to the more deadly force of a police handgun.

Police association president Sean Bambrick agreed, telling The Whig-Standard that he found Tasers "one of the best tools we have in terms of incapacitating the threat and having little to no injury to the person that you were dealing with at the time."

On May 3 of this year, city police once again used a Taser to bring down a patient on the psychiatric ward of Hotel Dieu Hospital. The 350-pound man was violent with hospital staff and even police couldn't subdue him. So he was lured onto an elevator and shot with a Taser, enabling police to handcuff him.
There are two troubling issues here.
First, are Tasers really as safe as studies indicate?
Second, are they appropriate for use in all situations?

No one wants to see police officers hurt in skirmishes with violent people. But if Tasers are defined as more humane alternatives to handguns and rifles, does that mean the next course of action in dealing with Samuel Truscott, a man high on cocaine, and the patient on the psychiatric ward, was to shoot them?
If electronic stun guns are just a new technology for controlling the mentally ill, that's a topic for wider social debate and concern.
